clue.text: Improve a chance acquaintance

explanation.surface: Making the most of someone met by chance.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick up is to recover or get better; a pick-up is also someone casually met and befriended.

clue.text: He turns crises to personal gain

definitions.text: He turns crises to personal gain

parts.words: He turns crises to personal gain
parts.note: a person who makes excessive money from shortages in wartime or emergencies

explanation.surface: A description of an opportunist who exploits emergencies.
explanation.definitionFit: A wartime speculator who makes excessive gains from scarcity exploits crises.

clue.text: Sheared at speed

explanation.surface: Sheep shorn very quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: Clipped means cut short with shears, and going at a fast clip means travelling quickly.

clue.text: One-sided but not necessarily partial

parts.note: acting on one side only, like a decision by one party, without being biased

explanation.surface: A note that a lopsided view need not be prejudiced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One-sided' suggests bias, but the clue says it need not be: the sense is action taken by one party alone.
explanation.definitionFit: An action taken by one party alone affects one side without being biased.

clue.text: Invitation to gather heather for keeps

parts.note: to gather flowers or fruit is to pick them
ling is another name for common heather

explanation.surface: Someone is invited out onto the moor to collect heather to keep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Invitation to' frames the two words as a call to 'pick ling!'; the definition is 'for keeps', preserving food in vinegar or brine so it lasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Preserving vegetables in vinegar is done so they will keep for a long time.

clue.text: " The sons Of Belial, flown with —— and wine " (Milton)

definitions.text: " The sons Of Belial, flown with —— and wine " (Milton)

parts.words: " The sons Of Belial, flown with —— and wine " (Milton)
parts.note: a line from Paradise Lost book one with a word removed; the sons are drunk on wine and on arrogance

explanation.surface: A quotation from Milton about riotous drunken revellers with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Paradise Lost, Book I: 'the sons Of Belial, flown with insolence and wine'; 'flown' means flushed or swollen.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is arrogant rudeness, which swells Belial's sons alongside wine.

clue.text: Where elders flourish

parts.note: elders are lay officials of the Presbyterian church, not trees, and they thrive in its places of worship

explanation.surface: A remark about where elder trees grow well.
explanation.walkthrough: Elders sound like elder trees, but they are church officers; KIRK is the Scottish word for a church, whose Presbyterian system is run by elders.
explanation.definitionFit: The Scottish church is governed by elders in Presbyterian fashion.

clue.text: Such eavesdroppers are thoroughly chilled

parts.note: eavesdroppers read literally are things that drop from the eaves of a roof, frozen ones here

explanation.surface: A remark that certain snoopers are frozen with fear.
explanation.walkthrough: An eavesdropper is a snoop, but read literally it is something dripping from the eaves; frozen drips hang there in winter.
explanation.definitionFit: Frozen drips hanging from the eaves are spikes of ice formed in cold weather.

clue.text: When wigs are here, there's trouble

definitions.text: When wigs are here, there's trouble

parts.words: When wigs are here, there's trouble
parts.note: the Irish idiom 'there'll be wigs on the' grassy place means a fight is coming

explanation.surface: A remark that lawyers in wigs mean trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wigs on the green' is an Irish phrase for a brawl, from wigs knocked off in fights on the village grass.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a village lawn or common, the grassy place where the fights took place.

clue.text: Troops' troupers

parts.note: the organisation that sent performers to entertain the armed forces in the Second World War

explanation.surface: Entertainers who perform for soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: ENSA was the Entertainments National Service Association, which put on shows for British forces.
explanation.definitionFit: The British wartime service supplied entertainers, or troupers, for the forces.

clue.text: Belief that love comes to the point when I get on

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, shaped like the letter O
a pin has a sharp point, so the point stands for pin

explanation.surface: Someone believes love only reaches its peak in later life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I get on' looks like ageing, but it simply gives I followed by ON.
explanation.definitionFit: A view a person holds is a belief they have formed.

clue.text: That of Cortez's men was wild

definitions.text: That of Cortez's men was wild

parts.words: That of Cortez's men was wild
parts.note: Keats's sonnet on Chapman's Homer has Cortez's men looking at each other with a wild guess on first seeing the Pacific

explanation.surface: A remark about the conquistadors' untamed behaviour.
explanation.walkthrough: Keats's poem 'On First Looking into Chapman's Homer' ends with the men looking 'at each other with a wild surmise'; the clue asks for the noun that 'wild' described.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats's line describes a wild guess, a conjecture on seeing the Pacific.

clue.text: I'm with a pal upset by a wire and not to be appeased

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

indicators.note: upset says the letters of the word pal are knocked over and rearranged

parts.note: a cable is a wire, and also a telegram sent by wire

explanation.surface: Someone, joined by a friend, is upset by a telegram and cannot be calmed.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'a's are link words: the one before 'pal' does not join the anagram, and 'a wire' is simply the cable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who cannot be pacified is relentless and unforgiving.

clue.text: "Up the airy mountain, Down the rushy ——" (Allingham)

definitions.text: "Up the airy mountain, Down the rushy ——" (Allingham)

parts.words: "Up the airy mountain, Down the rushy ——" (Allingham)
parts.note: the opening of William Allingham's poem The Fairies, with its last word left blank for the solver

explanation.surface: A quotation from an Irish poem about fairies with its final word missing.
explanation.walkthrough: William Allingham's 'The Fairies' begins 'Up the airy mountain, Down the rushy glen'; the missing word is the narrow valley.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's lowland opposite the mountain is a narrow Scottish or Irish valley.

clue.text: Virginia's up the wall !

parts.note: Virginia creeper climbs walls, and the clue names its botanical genus

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a woman called Virginia is going mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up the wall' means exasperated, but Virginia creeper literally climbs walls; it was classified as a species of this genus.
explanation.definitionFit: Virginia creeper, the climbing plant that covers walls, was placed in this botanical genus.

clue.text: The trivial round, no doubt is

definitions.text: The trivial round, no doubt is

parts.words: The trivial round, no doubt is
parts.note: Keble's hymn line 'The trivial round, the common task' is read as a daily routine, and anything round has no finish

explanation.surface: A weary comment that daily routine, as the hymn says, never stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The trivial round' is from John Keble's hymn about daily duties; a round, like a circle, has no stopping point, and neither does routine.
explanation.definitionFit: A circle and a daily routine both go on without a finish, so are unceasing.

clue.text: Eve strode about awkwardly as a loader

indicators.note: moved about awkwardly, the letters of these two words are clumsily rearranged

explanation.surface: Eve walks around clumsily, like a dock worker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about awkwardly' rearranges EVE STRODE.
explanation.definitionFit: A docker who loads and unloads cargo ships is a loader by trade.

clue.text: She seems in a muddle but you can't escape her

indicators.note: a muddle is a confused jumble, so the letters of seems in come out reordered

explanation.surface: A woman appears confused, yet nobody can get away from her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'She' looks like part of the fodder but is the start of the definition, the goddess you cannot escape; 'a muddle' rearranges SEEMS IN.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of retribution pursues wrongdoers until justice catches them.

clue.text: Entrance for the Artful Dodger?

parts.note: a dodger moves aside to avoid things, and a side door has steps leading to it

explanation.surface: A question about how Dickens's pickpocket gets into a building.
explanation.walkthrough: The Artful Dodger is the pickpocket in Dickens's Oliver Twist; a dodger evades, and the steps at a side door are his natural way in.
explanation.definitionFit: A dodger evades by stepping aside, and the steps at a side door are a discreet way in.

clue.text: Hues as seen through Mrs. Alexander's spectacles ?

definitions.text: Hues as seen through Mrs. Alexander's spectacles ?

parts.words: Hues as seen through Mrs. Alexander's spectacles ?
parts.note: the colour of the world seen through rose-tinted glasses, the optimistic view of the hymn writer Mrs Alexander

explanation.surface: A question about what colours the hymn writer saw through her glasses.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Cecil Frances Alexander wrote 'All Things Bright and Beautiful', an optimistic hymn; optimists see life through rose-coloured spectacles.
explanation.definitionFit: Rose-tinted means pinkish, the colour optimists are said to see everything in.

clue.text: Georgia rises in greeting to the saved

indicators.note: in puts one piece inside the greeting word

parts.note: salve is a Latin greeting, hail

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: GA is the abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

explanation.surface: Georgia stands to greet those who have been rescued.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'rises' reads the state's abbreviation from bottom to top; salve is the Latin word for 'hail', used as a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Goods rescued from a wreck or fire are what has been saved.

clue.text: Intercede, but not in this put-up arrangement

indicators.note: an arrangement is a reordering, so what is left of the letters is rearranged

parts.note: the word in is the part taken away from the longer word before the rest is reshuffled

explanation.surface: Someone intervenes, but not in this rigged scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but not in' removes IN from INTERCEDE, leaving TERCEDE, which 'arrangement' rearranges. 'put-up' looks like rigged, as in a put-up job, but it means raised.
explanation.definitionFit: Something built or raised upright, like a tent, has been set up.

clue.text: Commoners' platform ?

parts.note: a Roman officer elected to protect the plebeians, and also a raised speaking dais

explanation.surface: A question about a stage for ordinary people.
explanation.walkthrough: In Rome the tribune of the plebs championed the common people; the same word means a raised platform for speakers.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman officer stood for the plebeians, and the word also means a raised speaker's dais.

clue.text: Lily kept a diary, too !

parts.note: Lily is the heroine of Trollope's novels, and her surname is shared with Mrs ... of the BBC radio serial Mrs ... Diary

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a girl called Lily kept a journal as well.
explanation.walkthrough: Lily Dale is a heroine of Trollope's The Small House at Allington; 'Mrs Dale's Diary' was a long-running BBC radio serial, so a Dale kept a diary 'too'.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname shared by Trollope's Lily and the radio diarist Mrs Dale is also a valley.

clue.text: It's not to her credit that the girl has appeal

parts.note: a deb is a debutante, a girl coming out in society
it was slang for sex appeal, as in the It girl

explanation.surface: A debutante's sex appeal is no credit to her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'credit' makes the def read as a moral judgment; in accounts a debit is the entry opposite a credit.
explanation.definitionFit: In bookkeeping an entry on the opposite side to credit records money owed.

clue.text: They need a master on occasions

definitions.text: They need a master on occasions

parts.words: They need a master on occasions
parts.note: formal events are run by a master of ..., and occasions are formal events

explanation.surface: A remark that some people need someone in charge from time to time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on occasions' reads as 'sometimes', but the occasions are formal events, which are presided over by a master of ceremonies.
explanation.definitionFit: Formal rituals and observances at public occasions are run by a master of them.

clue.text: Send round for these objects

indicators.note: sending a letter round moves it from the front of the word to the back

explanation.surface: An instruction to dispatch someone to fetch some items.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round' moves the S of SEND to the back.
explanation.definitionFit: Aims or purposes are what one strives for, so they are objects in that sense.

clue.text: Bearded pal

parts.note: Shakespeare's soldier is 'bearded like the' ..., whose old name is also slang for a partner

explanation.surface: A friend with a beard.
explanation.walkthrough: Jaques's soldier in As You Like It is 'bearded like the pard', an old word for leopard; pard is also American slang for partner.
explanation.definitionFit: The old word for leopard, which Shakespeare calls bearded, doubles as slang for a partner.

clue.text: Short announcement amid applause from a Gascon ?

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: bravo is a cry of applause
an ad is a short form of advertisement, an announcement

explanation.surface: A Gascon makes a brief announcement over the cheering.
explanation.walkthrough: Gascons were proverbial braggarts (hence 'gasconade'), so the boastful show expected from one is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Gascons had a name for boasting, and bold swaggering show is the trait expected of them.

clue.text: Put inside perhaps, in argument

annotationWithheld.why: Put inside perhaps, in argument (7): DISPUTE needs PUT inside an anagram of SIDE, but SIDE is only in the word 'inside', which would have to be both the container indicator and the anagram fodder

clue.text: Where the seamstresses put their feet down ?

definitions.text: Where the seamstresses put their feet down ?

parts.words: Where the seamstresses put their feet down ?
parts.note: a sewing machine of the period was driven by foot pedals that the seamstress pressed

explanation.surface: A question about where dressmakers take a firm stand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put their feet down' sounds like being firm, but here it is literal: the foot pedals of an old sewing machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Foot-operated levers drove the old sewing machine, pressed down by the worker's feet.

clue.text: They bring trouble on themselves by request

definitions.text: They bring trouble on themselves by request

parts.words: They bring trouble on themselves by request
parts.note: people who make requests are said to be asking for trouble

explanation.surface: A remark about people who invite their own misfortune.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'asking for trouble' is read literally: the people who ask are the ones who get it.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who make requests or questions are people who ask.
